note: English text for the 460 catalogue questions, written for this app. BAMF publishes the Gesamtfragenkatalog in German only, so the German in src/data/questions.json is the authoritative text and everything here is a translation of it. context is a short explanation of the correct answer, shown under the answer in practice and review; BAMF publishes no equivalent, so these are written here too.

1.text: In Germany, people are allowed to say something openly against the government because …
options: people have the right to vote.
1.context: Freedom of expression (Article 5 of the Basic Law) lets anyone voice criticism of those in power without fear of punishment. Being able to contradict the government is exactly what separates a democracy from a dictatorship.

2.text: In Germany, parents can decide until their child is 14 whether it takes part at school in …
2.context: Religious education is the only school subject the Basic Law singles out: under Article 7, parents decide whether their child takes part, and from 14 the child decides for itself.

3.text: Germany is a state governed by the rule of law. What does that mean?
options: All residents and the state itself must obey the law.
The state does not have to obey the law.
Only Germans have to follow the law.
3.context: In a Rechtsstaat the law binds everyone, the state included. Officials, police and ministers are as subject to the law as any resident, and courts can be asked to enforce that.

4.text: Which right is one of the basic rights in Germany?
options: taking the law into your own hands
4.context: Freedom of expression is one of the basic rights in Articles 1 to 19 of the Basic Law. Owning weapons or settling scores yourself are not rights at all.

5.text: Elections in Germany are free. What does that mean?
options: You may accept money for voting for a particular candidate.
Only people who have never been in prison are allowed to vote.
Voters may be neither influenced nor forced to cast a particular vote, and must suffer no disadvantage from voting.
Everyone entitled to vote must vote.
5.context: Free means nobody may pressure, bribe or coerce you over your vote, and you may not be penalised for how you voted. It does not mean voting is compulsory, nor does a criminal record generally remove the right to vote.

6.text: What is the German constitution called?
6.context: The German constitution is called the Grundgesetz, or Basic Law. The name was chosen in 1949 as a deliberately provisional one, because the founders hoped for a joint constitution once Germany was reunited.

7.text: Which right is one of the basic rights guaranteed by the German constitution? The right to …
7.context: Freedom of faith and conscience is guaranteed by Article 4. Entertainment, work and housing are things the state may support, but they are not basic rights you can claim in court.

8.text: What is not in Germany's Basic Law?
options: Everyone should have the same amount of money.
Everyone is equal before the law.
8.context: The Basic Law guarantees dignity, free expression and equality before the law, but it never promises equal wealth. It sets the rules of the game, not the outcome.

9.text: Which basic right applies in Germany only to foreign nationals? The basic right to …
9.context: The right to asylum in Article 16a applies only to people who are not German citizens, which makes it the one basic right reserved for foreign nationals. Dignity and free expression apply to everybody.

10.text: What is compatible with Germany's Basic Law?
10.context: A fine is an ordinary criminal penalty and entirely compatible with the Basic Law. Corporal punishment, torture and the death penalty are all forbidden; Article 102 abolished capital punishment outright.

11.text: What is the constitution of the Federal Republic of Germany called?
11.context: It is the Grundgesetz, the Basic Law. It came into force on 23 May 1949 and, after reunification, became the constitution for the whole of Germany.

12.text: A party in the German Bundestag wants to abolish freedom of the press. Is that possible?
options: Yes, if more than half of the members of the Bundestag are in favour.
Yes, but two thirds of the members of the Bundestag must be in favour.
No, because freedom of the press is a basic right. It cannot be abolished.
No, because only the Bundesrat can abolish freedom of the press.
12.context: Freedom of the press is part of the basic rights, and Article 79(3) puts the core of those rights beyond the reach of any majority. Not even a unanimous Bundestag could abolish it.

13.text: In parliament, the term "opposition" stands for …
options: the parliamentary group with the most members.
all parties that cleared the 5% threshold at the last election.
all members who do not belong to the governing party or parties.
13.context: The opposition is made up of all members who do not belong to the governing party or parties. Its job is to scrutinise the government and offer an alternative.

14.text: Freedom of expression in Germany means that I …
options: may insult passers-by in the street.
can express my opinion on the internet.
may display Nazi, Hamas or Islamic State symbols in public.
may only express my opinion as long as I do not contradict the government.
14.context: Freedom of expression covers stating your opinion in public, including online. It does not protect insulting people or displaying the symbols of banned organisations.

15.text: What does Germany's Basic Law prohibit?
15.context: Article 12 of the Basic Law forbids forced labour. Choosing your occupation freely and working abroad are precisely the freedoms it protects.

16.text: When is freedom of expression restricted in Germany?
options: when false claims about individuals are spread in public
when opinions are expressed about the federal government
16.context: Free expression ends where it damages other people's rights, for example by spreading untrue factual claims about them. Criticising the government, the state or religion is fully protected.

options: unequal treatment of citizens by the state.
17.context: Article 3 obliges the state to treat people equally, so unequal treatment by the state is what the law forbids. Expression, petitions and assembly are rights the law guarantees, not bans.

18.text: Which basic right is guaranteed in Article 1 of the Basic Law of the Federal Republic of Germany?
18.context: Article 1 opens with the sentence "Human dignity shall be inviolable." It is placed first deliberately, as the foundation on which every other basic right rests.

19.text: What is meant by the right of "freedom of movement" in Germany?
options: You may choose where you live.
You may decide to follow a different religion.
You may go about in public only lightly dressed.
19.context: Freizügigkeit is the right to move to and settle anywhere in Germany. It is about choosing where you live, not about what you wear or which job you take.

20.text: A party in Germany pursues the aim of establishing a dictatorship. It is then …
options: committed to the rule of law.
20.context: A party aiming to set up a dictatorship works against the free democratic basic order and is therefore unconstitutional. Only the Federal Constitutional Court may ban a party on those grounds.

21.text: Which is the coat of arms of the Federal Republic of Germany?
21.context: The federal coat of arms is the black eagle on a golden shield. It has been in use since 1950 and goes back to the Weimar Republic's design.

22.text: What form of state does Germany have?
22.context: Germany is a republic: its head of state is elected, not born into the office. Republic, democracy, federal state and welfare state are all described in Article 20.

23.text: In Germany, most working people are …
options: working voluntarily for a federal state.
self-employed with a company of their own.
employed by a company or a public authority.
23.context: Most working people in Germany are employees of a company or a public authority rather than self-employed. Roughly nine in ten workers are in dependent employment.

24.text: How many federal states does the Federal Republic of Germany have?
24.context: Germany has 16 federal states. There were 11 in the West until 1990, when five eastern states joined and Berlin was reunited.

25.text: Which is not a federal state of the Federal Republic of Germany?
25.context: Alsace-Lorraine is a region of France, not a German federal state. The other three are all part of the 16.

options: a democratic and social federal state.
a social and socialist federal state.
26.context: Article 20 describes Germany as a democratic and social federal state. Democratic because power comes from the people, social because the state provides for those in need.

27.context: Germany is a federal state: power is shared between the federation and the 16 states, each with its own parliament and government.

28.text: Who elects the members of the Bundestag in Germany?
28.context: The members of the Bundestag are elected by the people entitled to vote. All state authority emanates from the people, and elections are how that happens.

29.text: Which animal is the heraldic animal of the Federal Republic of Germany?
29.context: The heraldic animal is the eagle. The Bundesadler appears on the coat of arms, on coins and in the plenary chamber of the Bundestag.

30.text: What is not a feature of our democracy?
30.context: Press censorship is the opposite of democracy; Article 5 states plainly that censorship shall not take place. Regular elections, free expression and several parties are all essential features.

31.text: In Germany, parties working together to form a government is called a …
31.context: When parties work together to form a government, that is a coalition. German governments are usually coalitions, because one party rarely wins a majority on its own.

32.text: What is not a branch of state power in Germany?
32.context: The press is not a branch of state power. The three branches are the legislature, the executive and the judiciary; the press is often called the "fourth estate", but it is private and independent of the state.

33.text: Which statement is correct? In Germany …
options: the state and religious communities are separate from one another.
the religious communities form the state.
the state depends on the religious communities.
the state and religious communities form a single unit.
33.context: In Germany the state and religious communities are separate. There is no state church, though churches do cooperate with the state in areas such as schools and welfare.

options: a state governed by the rule of law
34.context: Germany is not a monarchy. It is a democracy, a state governed by the rule of law and a welfare state, all at once.

35.text: How does the German state finance social insurance?
35.context: Social insurance is financed by contributions (Sozialabgaben) that employers and employees pay from wages. Church tax and donations fund quite different things.

36.text: Which measure creates social security in Germany?
36.context: Health insurance is one of the five branches of statutory social insurance and is what protects people financially when they fall ill. Car and buildings insurance are private cover for property.

37.text: What are the heads of government of most federal states in Germany called?
37.context: In most federal states the head of government is called Ministerpräsident. The three city states are the exception: Berlin has a Governing Mayor, Hamburg and Bremen a First Mayor and a President of the Senate.

38.text: The Federal Republic of Germany is a democratic and social …
38.context: Article 20 describes the Federal Republic as a democratic and social federal state. A confederation would be a looser association of independent states.

39.text: What does every German federal state have?
39.context: Every federal state has its own government, its own parliament and its own constitution. None has its own army, currency or foreign minister.

40.text: With which words does the German national anthem begin?
options: Völker, hört die Signale … (Peoples, hear the signals …)
Einigkeit und Recht und Freiheit … (Unity and justice and freedom …)
Freude schöner Götterfunken … (Joy, beautiful spark of the gods …)
40.context: The anthem is the third verse of the Deutschlandlied, beginning "Einigkeit und Recht und Freiheit" — unity and justice and freedom. Only that third verse is the national anthem.

41.text: Why is there more than one party in a democracy?
options: because this is how the differing opinions of citizens are represented
so that bribery in politics is kept in check
41.context: Several parties exist so that the different opinions among citizens can actually be represented. A single-party state cannot offer voters a genuine choice.

42.text: Who passes a new law in Germany?
42.context: Laws are passed by parliament — the Bundestag, with the Bundesrat taking part where the states are affected. The government may propose bills, but it cannot enact them.

43.text: When can a party be banned in Germany?
options: if its election campaign is too expensive
if it fights against the constitution
if it voices criticism of the head of state
if its programme proposes a new direction
43.context: A party may be banned only if it fights against the constitution, and only the Federal Constitutional Court can order it. Expensive campaigns or unpopular ideas are no grounds at all.

44.text: Whom can citizens in Germany not elect directly?
44.context: The Federal President is elected by the Federal Convention, not by the people. Members of the Bundestag, state parliaments and the European Parliament are all elected directly.

45.text: Which type of insurance does long-term care insurance belong to?
45.context: Long-term care insurance is one of the five branches of statutory social insurance, alongside health, pension, unemployment and accident insurance.

46.text: The German state has many tasks. Which one is among them?
options: It supplies all residents with newspapers free of charge.
46.context: Building roads and schools is a core task of the state. Producing cars or selling food is left to private business in a market economy.

47.text: The German state has many tasks. Which one is not among them?
options: It pays for holiday trips for all citizens.
47.context: The state pays child benefit and supports museums and athletes, but it does not pay for citizens' holidays. That is simply not a public task.

48.text: Which body is not one of Germany's constitutional bodies?
48.context: The citizens' assembly is not a constitutional body. The five are the Bundestag, the Bundesrat, the Federal President, the federal government and the Federal Constitutional Court.

49.text: Who determines school policy in Germany?
49.context: School policy is decided by the federal states, which is why curricula and school types differ from state to state. This is known as Kulturhoheit der Länder.

50.text: The economic system in Germany is called …
50.context: Germany's system is called the social market economy: supply and demand set prices, while the state provides a social safety net and rules for fair competition.

51.text: It is not part of a democratic state governed by the rule of law that …
options: people can speak critically about the government.
people are arrested by a private police force without reason.
someone commits a crime and is arrested for it.
51.context: Arrests without grounds by a private police force have no place in a state governed by the rule of law. Criticism, peaceful demonstrations and arrests following a crime are all perfectly normal.

52.text: What does "sovereignty of the people" mean? All state authority emanates from …
52.context: Article 20 says all state authority emanates from the people. Citizens exercise it through elections and votes, and through the organs of state they elect.

53.text: What does "state governed by the rule of law" mean in Germany?
options: The state must obey the law.
53.context: Rechtsstaat means the state itself is bound by the law. It has nothing to do with right-wing politics — "Recht" here means law, not the political right.

54.text: What is not a branch of state power in Germany?
54.context: There is no such branch as a "Direktive". The three branches of state power are the legislature, the executive and the judiciary.

options: the seat of the Bundestag in Berlin
the Federal Constitutional Court in Karlsruhe
55.context: The picture shows the Reichstag building in Berlin, the seat of the Bundestag since 1999. Its glass dome, open to visitors, has become a symbol of transparent government.

56.text: Which office belongs to municipal administration in Germany?
56.context: The Ordnungsamt, or public order office, is part of municipal administration. The tax office belongs to the state and the Federal Foreign Office to the federation.

57.text: Who is usually elected President of the German Bundestag?
options: the Minister-President of the largest federal state
a member of the largest parliamentary group
57.context: By long-standing convention the President of the Bundestag comes from the largest parliamentary group. The office ranks second in protocol after the Federal President.

58.text: Who appoints the ministers of the federal government in Germany?
options: the President of the Federal Constitutional Court
58.context: Federal ministers are formally appointed by the Federal President, on the proposal of the Chancellor. The Chancellor chooses them; the President signs the appointment.

59.text: How many years ago was there first a Jewish community in the territory of present-day Germany?
59.context: A decree of Emperor Constantine from the year 321 mentions a Jewish community in Cologne, so Jewish life on German soil is around 1,700 years old.

60.text: In Germany, the Bundestag and the Bundesrat belong to the …
60.context: The Bundestag and the Bundesrat both take part in making laws, so both belong to the legislature. The judiciary is the courts, the executive the government and administration.

61.text: What does "sovereignty of the people" mean?
options: The king or queen rules over the people.
The Federal Constitutional Court stands above the constitution.
Interest groups exercise sovereignty together with the government.
State authority emanates from the people.
61.context: Sovereignty of the people means state authority emanates from the people. It is the answer to the old idea that power belongs to a monarch by birth.

62.text: When the parliament of a German federal state is elected, this is called a …
62.context: Electing the parliament of a federal state is a Landtagswahl. Local elections choose municipal councils; the Bundestag election chooses the federal parliament.

63.text: What is not part of the executive in Germany?
63.context: The courts are the judiciary, not the executive. The executive is the government together with the administration that carries out the law, such as the police and the tax office.

64.text: The Federal Republic of Germany today is divided into …
options: an eastern state and a western state.
64.context: Germany is organised in three tiers: the federation, the states and the municipalities. The four occupation zones and the division into two states are long gone.

65.text: It is not one of the tasks of the German Bundestag to …
65.context: Forming the cabinet is the Chancellor's job, not the Bundestag's. The Bundestag drafts and passes laws, scrutinises the government and elects the Chancellor.

66.text: Which cities have the largest Jewish communities in Germany?
66.context: Berlin and Munich have the largest Jewish communities in Germany today. Worms and Speyer were great medieval centres, but their communities are small now.

67.text: What is above all a task of the federal states in Germany?
67.context: School policy is above all a matter for the federal states. Defence, foreign affairs and the main lines of economic policy belong to the federation.

68.text: Why does the state supervise the school system in Germany?
options: because there are only state schools in Germany
because all pupils must have a school-leaving qualification
because there are different schools in the federal states
because under the Basic Law it is its task
68.context: Article 7 of the Basic Law places the entire school system under state supervision. That is why the state sets standards even for private schools.

69.text: The Federal Republic of Germany has a three-tier administrative structure. What is the lowest political tier called?
69.context: The lowest tier is the municipality, the Gemeinde. Above it come the federal state and then the federation.

70.text: German Federal President Gustav Heinemann hands Helmut Schmidt the certificate of appointment as German Federal Chancellor in 1974. What is one of the tasks of the German Federal President?
options: They conduct the business of government.
They propose the Chancellor for election.
70.context: The Federal President proposes a candidate for Chancellor to the Bundestag and then appoints the person elected, as in the photo. Running the government is the Chancellor's job, not the President's.

71.text: Where does the German Federal Chancellor spend most time? Most often they are …
options: in Bonn, because the Federal Chancellery and the Bundestag are there.
at Meseberg Palace, the federal government's guest house, to receive state guests.
at Bellevue Palace, the official residence of the Federal President, to receive state guests.
in Berlin, because the Federal Chancellery and the Bundestag are there.
71.context: The Chancellor spends most time in Berlin, where both the Federal Chancellery and the Bundestag are. Meseberg and Bellevue are used only occasionally, and Bellevue is the President's residence.

72.text: What is the name of Germany's current Federal Chancellor?
72.context: Friedrich Merz has been Federal Chancellor since 2025. He is the tenth person to hold the office since 1949.

73.text: The two largest parliamentary groups in the German Bundestag are currently …
73.context: After the 2025 federal election the two largest groups in the Bundestag are the CDU/CSU and the AfD. The largest group normally provides the President of the Bundestag.

74.text: What is the parliament for the whole of Germany called?
74.context: The parliament for the whole of Germany is the Bundestag. The Volkskammer was the GDR's parliament and no longer exists.

75.text: What is the name of Germany's current head of state?
75.context: Frank-Walter Steinmeier has been Federal President, and thus head of state, since 2017. He was re-elected for a second term in 2022.

76.text: What does the abbreviation CDU stand for in Germany?
options: Club Deutscher Unternehmer (Club of German Entrepreneurs)
Christlicher Deutscher Umweltschutz (Christian German Environmental Protection)
76.context: CDU stands for Christlich Demokratische Union, the Christian Democratic Union. It has been one of the two big parties since 1949.

77.context: The Bundeswehr is Germany's armed forces, founded in 1955. It is a parliamentary army: deployments abroad need the Bundestag's approval.

78.text: What does the abbreviation SPD stand for?
options: Sozialistische Partei Deutschlands (Socialist Party of Germany)
Sozialpolitische Partei Deutschlands (Social Policy Party of Germany)
Sozialdemokratische Partei Deutschlands (Social Democratic Party of Germany)
Sozialgerechte Partei Deutschlands (Socially Just Party of Germany)
78.context: SPD stands for Sozialdemokratische Partei Deutschlands, the Social Democratic Party. Founded in 1863, it is Germany's oldest party.

79.text: What does the abbreviation FDP stand for in Germany?
79.context: FDP stands for Freie Demokratische Partei, the Free Democratic Party, which stands in the liberal tradition.

80.text: Which court in Germany is responsible for interpreting the Basic Law?
80.context: The Federal Constitutional Court in Karlsruhe interprets the Basic Law. It can strike down laws and is the final authority on basic rights.

81.text: Who elects the Federal Chancellor in Germany?
81.context: The Chancellor is elected by the Bundestag, on the Federal President's proposal. Voters choose the Bundestag, and the Bundestag chooses the Chancellor.

82.text: Who chairs the German federal cabinet?
82.context: The Chancellor chairs the federal cabinet and sets the general policy guidelines — the Richtlinienkompetenz of Article 65.

83.text: Who elects the German Federal Chancellor?
83.context: It is the Bundestag that elects the Chancellor. The Federal Convention has only one job: electing the Federal President.

84.text: What is the main task of the German Federal President? They …
84.context: The Federal President represents the country at home and abroad. The office is largely ceremonial, standing above day-to-day party politics.

85.text: Who makes up the German Bundesrat?
options: the ministers of the federal government
the government representatives of the federal states
85.context: The Bundesrat is made up of members of the state governments, not of elected delegates. Through it the states take part in federal legislation.

86.text: Who elects the Federal President in Germany?
86.context: The Federal President is elected by the Federal Convention, which consists of all members of the Bundestag plus an equal number of delegates chosen by the state parliaments.

87.text: Who is the head of state of the Federal Republic of Germany?
87.context: The head of state is the Federal President. The Chancellor is head of government, which is a different role.

88.text: The parliamentary opposition in the German Bundestag …
options: decides who becomes a federal minister.
determines who sits in the Bundesrat.
proposes the heads of government of the federal states.
88.context: The opposition's central task is to scrutinise the government, question its decisions and offer alternatives. Appointing ministers is not its business.

89.text: What is the association of members of one party in parliament called in Germany?
89.context: Members of one party in parliament form a Fraktion, a parliamentary group. Group status brings rights such as committee seats and speaking time.

90.text: The German federal states take part in federal legislation through …
90.context: The states take part in federal legislation through the Bundesrat. Many laws cannot come into force without its consent.

91.text: In Germany, a change of government in a federal state can affect federal politics. Governing becomes …
options: more difficult if this changes the majority in the Bundestag.
easier if this brings new parties into the Bundesrat.
more difficult if this changes the majority in the Bundesrat.
easier if it is a wealthy federal state.
91.context: State governments send their representatives to the Bundesrat, so a change of government in one state can shift the majority there and make governing harder for the federal government.

92.text: What does the abbreviation CSU stand for in Germany?
options: Christlich Süddeutsche Union (Christian South German Union)
Christlich Sozialer Unternehmerverband (Christian Social Employers' Association)
92.context: CSU stands for Christlich Soziale Union, the Christian Social Union. It stands only in Bavaria, where the CDU does not compete.

93.text: The more "second votes" a party receives in a Bundestag election, the …
options: fewer first votes it can have.
more of the party's direct candidates enter parliament.
greater the risk of having to form a coalition.
more seats the party gets in parliament.
93.context: The second vote decides how many seats a party gets in the Bundestag, which makes it the more important of the two votes.

94.text: From what age may you take part in the election of the German Bundestag?
94.context: You may vote in Bundestag elections from the age of 18. Some states allow 16-year-olds to vote locally, but not federally.

95.text: What applies to most children in Germany?
95.context: School attendance is compulsory for most children in Germany, usually for nine or ten years. Voting is a right, not a duty.

96.text: How can someone who denies the Holocaust be punished?
options: up to 100 hours of community service
not at all, Holocaust denial is permitted
with a prison sentence of up to five years or a fine
96.context: Denying the Holocaust is a criminal offence under section 130 of the Criminal Code, punishable by up to five years in prison or a fine.

97.text: What do you pay automatically in Germany if you are in permanent employment?
97.context: Anyone in permanent employment automatically pays social insurance contributions, deducted from wages along with income tax.

98.text: If members of the German Bundestag change their parliamentary group, …
options: they may no longer take part in sittings of parliament.
the government can lose its majority.
the Federal President must give their consent beforehand.
the voters of those members may vote again.
98.context: Members keep their seats if they switch groups, so the government can lose its majority. Members are bound only by their conscience, not by party instructions.

99.text: Who pays for social insurance in Germany?
99.context: Social insurance is paid jointly by employers and employees, who each carry roughly half the contributions.

100.text: What is not part of statutory social insurance?
100.context: Life insurance is private cover, not part of statutory social insurance. The statutory branches are health, pension, unemployment, long-term care and accident insurance.

101.text: Trade unions are interest groups representing …
101.context: Trade unions represent employees. Employers have their own organisations, and the two sides negotiate collective agreements with each other.

102.text: What can you be honoured with in the Federal Republic of Germany for outstanding achievement in political, economic, cultural, intellectual or social life? With the …
options: honorary title "Hero of the German Democratic Republic"
102.context: The Bundesverdienstkreuz, the Federal Cross of Merit, is the highest general honour the Federal Republic awards. It is given for outstanding service to the country.

103.text: What is referred to in Germany as a "traffic light coalition"? The cooperation …
options: of the Bundestag groups of the CDU and the CSU
of the SPD, the FDP and Bündnis 90/Die Grünen in a government
of the CSU, Die LINKE and Bündnis 90/Die Grünen in a government
of the Bundestag groups of the CDU and the SPD
103.context: A "traffic light" coalition is one of SPD (red), FDP (yellow) and the Greens — the colours of a traffic light. Germany had such a government from 2021 to 2024.

104.text: A woman in Germany loses her job. What may not be the reason for this dismissal?
options: The woman has been ill and unable to work for a long time.
The woman was often late for work.
The woman deals with private matters during working hours.
The woman is having a baby and her boss knows this.
104.context: Dismissing a woman because she is pregnant is forbidden by the Maternity Protection Act. Poor timekeeping or private business in work time can be legitimate grounds.

105.text: What is one task of election helpers in Germany?
options: They help elderly people cast their vote in the polling booth.
They write the polling cards before the election.
They pass interim results on to the media.
They count the votes after the election closes.
105.context: Election helpers count the votes once polling closes. They must not influence voters or leak interim results.

106.text: In Germany, volunteer election helpers assist with elections. What is one task of election helpers?
options: They help children and elderly people to vote.
They write cards and letters stating the polling station.
They pass interim results on to journalists.
They count the votes after the election closes.
106.context: Volunteer election helpers run the polling station and count the votes afterwards. Their work is what makes the count public and verifiable.

107.text: For how many years is the Bundestag elected in Germany?
107.context: The Bundestag is elected for four years. An early election is possible but rare.

108.text: In a Bundestag election in Germany, anyone may vote who …
options: lives in the Federal Republic of Germany and wants to vote.
is a citizen of the Federal Republic of Germany and is at least 18 years old.
has lived in the Federal Republic of Germany for at least 3 years.
is a citizen of the Federal Republic of Germany and is at least 21 years old.
108.context: You may vote in a Bundestag election if you are a German citizen and at least 18 years old. Residence alone is not enough.

109.text: How often are Bundestag elections normally held in Germany?
109.context: Bundestag elections are normally held every four years, matching the parliament's term.

110.text: For how many years is the Bundestag elected in Germany?
110.context: The Bundestag's term is four years, after which it must face the voters again.

111.text: Which actions relating to the State of Israel are prohibited in Germany?
options: flying an Israeli flag on private property
publicly calling for the destruction of Israel
111.context: Publicly calling for the destruction of Israel is a criminal offence in Germany. Criticising Israeli government policy, by contrast, is covered by freedom of expression.

112.context: Elections in Germany are secret: nobody may find out how you voted. That is why polling booths and sealed ballot boxes exist.

113.text: Elections in Germany are won by the party that …
options: the majority of men voted for.
received the most votes among workers.
received the most first votes for its candidate for Chancellor.
113.context: The party with the most votes wins the election. Every vote counts the same, regardless of the voter's sex or occupation.

114.text: Taking part in democratic elections in Germany is …
114.context: Voting is a right, not a duty. There is no compulsory voting in Germany, and nobody may be penalised for staying at home.

115.text: What does "active right to vote" mean in Germany?
options: You have to go and vote.
You have to attend the counting of the votes.
115.context: The active right to vote is the right to cast a vote. The right to stand for election is the passive right to vote.

116.text: If you are allowed to vote in a Bundestag election in Germany, this is called …
116.context: Being allowed to vote is the active right to vote, which you have as a German citizen from the age of 18.

117.text: What is the minimum percentage of second votes a party must receive to be elected to the German Bundestag?
117.context: A party needs at least 5% of the second votes to enter the Bundestag, unless it wins enough constituency seats directly.

118.text: Who may become a member of the roughly 40 Jewish Maccabi sports clubs?
118.context: The Maccabi sports clubs are Jewish in tradition but open to everyone, whatever their religion or nationality.

119.text: Elections in Germany are free. What does that mean?
options: All convicted offenders are not allowed to vote.
If I want to go and vote, my employer must give me time off.
Every person can decide without coercion whether they want to vote and whom they want to vote for.
I can freely decide where I want to go and vote.
119.context: Free elections mean each person decides without coercion whether to vote at all and whom to vote for.

120.text: The electoral system in Germany is …
options: a majority and proportional representation system.
120.context: Germany combines both systems: constituency seats are decided by simple majority, while the overall distribution of seats follows proportional representation.

121.text: A party wants to enter the German Bundestag. But it must have a minimum share of the votes. This is called …
121.context: The minimum share of votes needed is called the 5% threshold, the Fünfprozenthürde. It is meant to keep parliament workable.

122.text: Which principles govern elections in Germany? Elections in Germany are …
122.context: The 5% threshold is the minimum share of the votes a party must reach to enter parliament.

123.text: What is the "5% threshold" in Germany?
options: a voting rule in the Bundestag for small parties
an attendance check in the Bundestag for votes
the minimum share of votes needed to enter parliament
an attendance check in the Bundesrat for votes
123.context: The 5% threshold is not a rule about voting inside parliament — it decides who gets into parliament in the first place.

124.text: The Bundestag election in Germany is the election of …
options: the parliaments of the federal states.
124.context: The Bundestag election elects the parliament for Germany. The Chancellor is then chosen by that parliament, not directly by voters.

125.text: In a democracy, one function of regular elections is …
options: to force citizens to cast their vote.
to make a change of government possible according to the will of the majority of voters.
to keep the country's existing laws in place.
to give more power to the poor.
125.context: Regular elections let the majority change the government peacefully. That possibility of a change of power is the heart of democracy.

126.text: What do citizens entitled to vote receive in Germany before an election?
options: a polling card from the municipality
permission to vote from the Federal President
a notification from the Federal Convention
a notification from the parish office
126.context: Before an election, voters receive a polling card from their municipality telling them where and when to vote.

127.text: Why is there a 5% threshold in the electoral law of the Federal Republic of Germany? It exists because …
options: the programmes of many small parties have a lot in common.
citizens can lose their bearings when there are many small parties.
many small parties make forming a government more difficult.
the small parties do not have enough money to pay the politicians.
127.context: The threshold exists because a parliament split among many small parties makes forming a stable government difficult. The Weimar Republic's experience is the historical reason.

128.text: Members of parliament elected by the citizens are called …
128.context: Members of parliament elected by citizens are called Abgeordnete, deputies. They represent the whole people, not just their own voters.

129.text: In Germany, the body elected by the people is …
options: the Minister-President of a federal state.
129.context: Of these, only the Bundestag is elected directly by the people. The Chancellor, the President and the state premiers are all elected by other bodies.

130.text: Which ballot paper would be valid in a Bundestag election? Based on the Federal Electoral Regulations (BWO), Annex 26
130.context: A valid ballot has exactly one cross in each column — one first vote and one second vote. More than one mark in a column makes that vote invalid.

131.context: A Bürgermeister is the head of a municipality. In most states the post is filled by direct election.

132.text: Many people in Germany do voluntary work in their free time. What does that mean?
options: They work voluntarily and unpaid in clubs and associations.
They work in the federal government.
They work in a hospital and earn money doing so.
132.context: Voluntary work, Ehrenamt, means giving your time unpaid to clubs, associations and charities. Millions of people in Germany do it.

133.text: What is permitted in Bundestag and state parliament elections in Germany?
options: A husband also votes for his wife.
You can cast your vote by postal ballot.
You can cast your vote by telephone on election day.
Children aged 14 and over may vote.
133.context: Postal voting is allowed in Bundestag and state elections and needs no special reason. Voting by phone, or on someone else's behalf, is not permitted.

134.text: There are plans to scrap the bus route you always take to work. What can you do to keep the bus route?
options: I take part in a citizens' initiative to keep the bus route, or start an initiative myself.
I join a sports club and train for cycling.
I contact the tax office, because as a taxpayer I have a right to the bus route.
I write a letter to the municipal forestry office.
134.context: Starting or joining a citizens' initiative is the normal way to press for a local decision to be changed. It is an everyday use of the freedom of assembly.

135.text: Whom do the trade unions represent in Germany?
135.context: Trade unions represent employees in dealings with employers, above all in negotiating pay and working conditions.

136.text: In Germany you go to the labour court in the case of …
136.context: The labour court handles disputes between employees and employers, including unfair dismissal. Neighbours and traffic accidents belong elsewhere.

137.text: Which court is responsible for conflicts in working life in Germany?
137.context: Conflicts in working life go to the Arbeitsgericht, the labour court. The first instance is free of court fees.

138.text: What can I do in Germany if my employer has dismissed me unlawfully?
options: keep working and be friendly to the boss
bring debt recovery proceedings against the employer
file an action for unfair dismissal
report the employer to the police
138.context: You can bring an action for unfair dismissal, a Kündigungsschutzklage. It must be filed within three weeks of receiving the notice.

139.text: When does a court trial take place in Germany? When someone …
options: has committed a criminal offence and is charged.
holds a different opinion from the government's.
has parked their car wrongly and it is towed away.
139.context: A criminal trial follows when someone is charged with an offence. Changing religion or having a car towed does not lead to a trial.

140.text: What does a lay judge do in Germany? They …
options: decide on guilt and sentence together with the judges.
140.context: Lay judges, Schöffen, sit alongside professional judges and decide with them on guilt and sentence. They are ordinary citizens, not lawyers.

141.text: Who advises people on legal questions in Germany and represents them in court?
141.context: A lawyer, Rechtsanwalt, advises people on legal questions and represents them in court. Judges decide cases; prosecutors bring charges.

142.text: What is the main task of a judge in Germany? A judge …
options: works at a court and delivers judgments.
looks after young people in court.
142.context: A judge works at a court and delivers judgments. Judges are independent and bound only by the law.

143.text: A judge in Germany belongs to the …
143.context: Judges belong to the judiciary, the Judikative — the branch of state power that applies the law to individual cases.

144.text: In Germany, a judge belongs to the …
144.context: The judiciary is the rechtsprechende Gewalt, the judicial power. The executive carries out the law; the legislature makes it.

145.text: In Germany, state power is divided. Which branch of state power does a judge work for? For the …
145.context: A judge works for the judiciary. The separation of powers keeps courts independent of government and parliament.

146.text: What is a set of proceedings before a court called in Germany?
146.context: Court proceedings are called a Prozess. Criminal, civil and labour cases all follow their own procedural rules.

147.text: What is a judge's work in Germany?
147.context: A judge's work is to administer justice — Recht sprechen. Making laws is parliament's job.

148.text: What is one task of the police in Germany?
options: to monitor compliance with the laws
148.context: The police monitor compliance with the law, prevent danger and investigate offences. Defending the country is the Bundeswehr's task.

149.text: What is an example of antisemitic behaviour?
149.context: Denying the Holocaust is antisemitic and a criminal offence. Criticising the Israeli government or attending a Jewish festival is not antisemitic.

150.text: A lay judge at a court in Germany is …
options: the deputy of the head of the town.
a member of a municipal council.
a person who has studied law.
150.context: A Schöffe is a volunteer judge, an ordinary citizen who serves for a fixed term. No legal training is required.

151.text: Who built the Wall in Berlin?
151.context: The GDR built the Berlin Wall in 1961 to stop its citizens leaving for the West. At least 140 people died at the Wall.

152.text: When were the National Socialists under Adolf Hitler in power in Germany?
152.context: The National Socialists were in power from 1933 to 1945, from Hitler's appointment as Chancellor to the end of the war.

options: the start of the building of the Berlin Wall
the election of Konrad Adenauer as Federal Chancellor
the end of the Second World War in Europe
153.context: 8 May 1945 is the day the Second World War ended in Europe, following Germany's unconditional surrender. It is remembered as the day of liberation.

154.text: When did the Second World War end?
154.context: The Second World War ended in 1945 — in Europe in May, and in Asia in September.

155.text: When were the National Socialists in power in Germany?
155.context: The Nazi dictatorship lasted twelve years, from 1933 to 1945.

156.text: In which year did Hitler become Reich Chancellor?
156.context: Hitler was appointed Reich Chancellor on 30 January 1933. Within months the regime had dismantled democracy.

157.text: In 1933 the National Socialists under Adolf Hitler established in Germany …
157.context: In 1933 the National Socialists established a dictatorship. Parties were banned, parliament disempowered and opponents persecuted.

158.context: The "Third Reich" was a dictatorship with one party, no free elections and no independent courts.

159.text: What did not exist in Germany during the period of National Socialism?
159.context: There were no free elections under National Socialism. Censorship, arbitrary arrests and the persecution of Jews were all part of the regime.

160.context: The Second World War lasted from 1939 to 1945. It began with the German attack on Poland on 1 September 1939.

161.text: What characterised the Nazi state? A policy …
161.context: The Nazi state was built on state racism: people were ranked by supposed race, and this led to persecution and to the murder of six million Jews.

162.text: Claus Schenk Graf von Stauffenberg became known for …
options: a gold medal at the 1936 Olympic Games.
the construction of the Reichstag building.
the assassination attempt on Hitler on 20 July 1944.
162.context: Stauffenberg led the attempt to assassinate Hitler on 20 July 1944. He was executed the same night and is remembered as a symbol of German resistance.

163.text: In which year did the National Socialists destroy synagogues and Jewish businesses in Germany?
163.context: In November 1938 the National Socialists destroyed synagogues and Jewish businesses across Germany in the pogrom known as the November pogroms.

164.text: What happened on 9 November 1938 in Germany?
options: The Second World War begins with the attack on Poland.
The National Socialists lose an election and dissolve the Reichstag.
Jewish businesses and synagogues are destroyed by National Socialists and their supporters.
Hitler becomes Reich President and has all parties banned.
164.context: On 9 November 1938, synagogues and Jewish shops were burned and looted throughout Germany. The date marks the shift from exclusion to open violence.

165.text: What was the name of the first Federal Chancellor of the Federal Republic of Germany?
165.context: Konrad Adenauer was the first Federal Chancellor, in office from 1949 to 1963.

166.text: At which demonstrations in Germany did people chant "We are the people"?
options: at the workers' uprising of 1953 in the GDR
at the demonstrations of 1968 in the Federal Republic of Germany
at the anti-nuclear demonstrations of 1985 in the Federal Republic of Germany
at the Monday demonstrations of 1989 in the GDR
166.context: "Wir sind das Volk" was chanted at the Monday demonstrations in the GDR in 1989. The peaceful protests helped bring down the regime.

167.text: Which countries were referred to in Germany as the "Allied occupying powers" after the Second World War?
options: Soviet Union, Great Britain, Poland, Sweden
USA, Soviet Union, Great Britain, France
167.context: The four Allied occupying powers were the USA, the Soviet Union, Great Britain and France. Each administered one zone.

168.text: Which country was not an "Allied occupying power" in Germany?
168.context: Japan was not an occupying power in Germany — it was on the other side of the war and was itself occupied afterwards.

169.text: When was the Federal Republic of Germany founded?
169.context: The Federal Republic of Germany was founded in 1949, when the Basic Law came into force on 23 May.

170.text: What existed in Germany during the period of National Socialism?
options: the right to free development of one's personality
170.context: Under National Socialism parties were banned; from July 1933 only the NSDAP remained. Press freedom and human dignity were abolished, not protected.

171.text: Social market economy means that the economy …
options: regulates itself solely by supply and demand.
is planned and directed by the state, and supply and demand are not taken into account.
follows supply and demand, but the state provides for social balance.
171.context: In a social market economy prices follow supply and demand, but the state provides a social balance through insurance, benefits and employment law.

172.text: In which occupation zone was the GDR founded? In the …
172.context: The GDR was founded in the Soviet occupation zone in October 1949, a few months after the Federal Republic.

173.text: The Federal Republic of Germany is a founding member …
options: of the North Atlantic Treaty Organisation (NATO).
173.context: Germany was one of the founding members of the European Union. It joined NATO in 1955 and the United Nations in 1973.

174.context: The GDR was founded in 1949 and existed until German reunification in 1990.

175.text: How many occupation zones were there in Germany after the Second World War?
175.context: Germany was divided into four occupation zones after the war, one for each of the Allied powers.

176.text: How were Germany's occupation zones distributed after 1945?
176.context: The British zone was in the north-west, the Soviet zone in the east, the American zone in the south and the French zone in the south-west.

177.text: Which German city was divided into four sectors after the Second World War?
177.context: Berlin was divided into four sectors, one for each occupying power, even though it lay inside the Soviet zone.

178.text: From June 1948 to May 1949 the citizens of West Berlin were supplied by an airlift. What circumstance was responsible for this?
options: For France, supplying the West Berlin population by aircraft was cheaper.
The American soldiers were afraid of raids during overland transport.
For Great Britain, supplying the city by airlift was quicker.
The Soviet Union cut off all traffic by land.
178.context: The Soviet Union blocked all land routes to West Berlin, so the Western Allies supplied the city by air for almost a year.

179.text: How did the Second World War in Europe officially end?
options: with the death of Adolf Hitler
with the unconditional surrender of Germany
with the withdrawal of the Germans from the occupied territories
179.context: The war in Europe ended officially with Germany's unconditional surrender in May 1945.

180.text: The first Federal Chancellor of the Federal Republic of Germany was …
180.context: Konrad Adenauer was the first Federal Chancellor and shaped the young republic's western orientation.

181.text: What did Willy Brandt want to express by kneeling in the former Jewish ghetto in Warsaw in 1970?
options: He submitted himself to the former Allies.
He asked Poland and the Polish Jews for forgiveness.
He showed his humility before the Warsaw Pact.
He said a prayer at the Tomb of the Unknown Soldier.
181.context: By kneeling at the memorial in the Warsaw ghetto in 1970, Willy Brandt asked Poland and Polish Jews for forgiveness for German crimes. The gesture became world-famous.

182.text: What is the Jewish house of prayer called?
182.context: The Jewish house of prayer is the synagogue. A mosque is Muslim, a church and a basilica Christian.

183.text: When was the "economic miracle" in the Federal Republic of Germany?
183.context: The "economic miracle" was the rapid post-war recovery of the 1950s, when the West German economy grew quickly and unemployment nearly vanished.

184.text: On what legal basis was the State of Israel founded?
options: a decision of the Zionist Congress
a proposal by the German federal government
184.context: The State of Israel was founded on the basis of a United Nations resolution, the partition plan of November 1947. Israel declared independence in May 1948.

185.text: What did the term "Iron Curtain" stand for? For the sealing off …
options: of the Warsaw Pact from the West
of northern Germany from southern Germany
of Nazi Germany from the Allies
185.context: The "Iron Curtain" described the sealing off of the Warsaw Pact states from the West during the Cold War.

186.text: In 1953 there was an uprising in the GDR which was commemorated for a long time by a public holiday in the Federal Republic of Germany. When was it?
186.context: The uprising of 17 June 1953 in the GDR was commemorated in West Germany as a public holiday until 1990.

187.text: Which German state had a black-red-gold flag with a hammer, a pair of compasses and a ring of grain?
187.context: The GDR's flag was black-red-gold with a hammer, a pair of compasses and a ring of grain in the middle, added in 1959.

188.text: In which year was the Wall built in Berlin?
188.context: The Wall was built in 1961, sealing off West Berlin almost overnight on 13 August.

189.text: When did the GDR build the Wall in Berlin?
189.context: The GDR began building the Berlin Wall on 13 August 1961.

190.text: What does the abbreviation DDR stand for?
190.context: DDR stands for Deutsche Demokratische Republik, the German Democratic Republic — the East German state from 1949 to 1990.

191.text: When was the Wall in Berlin opened to everyone?
191.context: The Wall was opened on 9 November 1989, after weeks of peaceful protest in the GDR.

192.text: Which of today's German federal states formerly belonged to the territory of the GDR?
192.context: Brandenburg was part of the GDR. Bavaria, Saarland and Hesse were always in the West.

193.context: From 1961 to 1989 Berlin was divided by the Wall, which separated families and friends for 28 years.

194.text: On 3 October, Germany celebrates the Day of German …
194.context: 3 October is the Day of German Unity, the national holiday. It marks the day in 1990 when the GDR acceded to the Federal Republic.

195.text: Which of today's German federal states formerly belonged to the territory of the GDR?
195.context: Saxony-Anhalt was one of the five states re-established on GDR territory in 1990.

196.text: Why is the period in autumn 1989 in the GDR called "Die Wende" (the turning point)? During this time the GDR changed politically …
options: from a dictatorship to a democracy.
from a liberal market economy to socialism.
from a monarchy to social democracy.
from a religious state to a communist state.
196.context: "Die Wende" describes the change from dictatorship to democracy in the GDR in autumn 1989, driven by peaceful mass protest.

197.text: Which of today's German federal states formerly belonged to the territory of the GDR?
197.context: Thuringia belonged to the GDR and became a federal state again in 1990.

198.text: Which of today's German federal states formerly belonged to the territory of the GDR?
198.context: Saxony was part of the GDR and is today one of the five eastern federal states.

199.text: In the GDR, the abbreviation "Stasi" referred to …
199.context: "Stasi" was short for Ministerium für Staatssicherheit, the GDR's Ministry for State Security.

200.text: Which of today's German federal states formerly belonged to the territory of the GDR?
200.context: Mecklenburg-Western Pomerania lay in the GDR, on the Baltic coast.

201.text: Which of the following lists contains only federal states that belonged to the territory of the former GDR?
options: Lower Saxony, North Rhine-Westphalia, Hesse, Schleswig-Holstein, Brandenburg
Mecklenburg-Western Pomerania, Brandenburg, Saxony, Saxony-Anhalt, Thuringia
Saxony, Thuringia, Hesse, Lower Saxony, Brandenburg
201.context: The five states on former GDR territory are Mecklenburg-Western Pomerania, Brandenburg, Saxony, Saxony-Anhalt and Thuringia.

202.text: Which side did the GDR belong to in the "Cold War"?
202.context: In the Cold War the GDR belonged to the Eastern bloc and to the Warsaw Pact, led by the Soviet Union.

203.text: What was the GDR's economic system called?
203.context: The GDR had a planned economy: the state decided what was produced, in what quantity and at what price.

204.text: How did the Federal Republic of Germany and the GDR become one state?
options: The Federal Republic occupied the GDR.
Today's five eastern federal states acceded to the Federal Republic of Germany.
The western federal states acceded to the GDR.
The GDR occupied the Federal Republic of Germany.
204.context: The five eastern states acceded to the Federal Republic in 1990 under Article 23 of the Basic Law. Unification was an accession, not a conquest.

205.text: With the accession of the GDR to the Federal Republic of Germany, the new federal states now also belong …
205.context: With reunification the new federal states also became part of what is now the European Union, without a separate accession procedure.

206.text: What do the so-called "Stolpersteine" (stumbling stones) in Germany commemorate?
206.context: Stolpersteine are small brass plaques set into pavements outside the last freely chosen homes of people persecuted and murdered under National Socialism.

207.text: Which military alliance was the GDR a member of?
207.context: The GDR was a member of the Warsaw Pact, the military alliance of the Eastern bloc.

options: the secret service in the "Third Reich"
the secret service of the GDR
a German sports club during the Second World War
208.context: The Stasi was the GDR's secret service. It kept files on millions of people and relied on a vast network of informers.

209.text: Which was the coat of arms of the German Democratic Republic?
209.context: The GDR's coat of arms showed a hammer and a pair of compasses within a ring of grain, standing for workers, intelligentsia and farmers.

210.text: What happened on 17 June 1953 in the GDR?
options: the ceremonial accession to the Warsaw Pact
nationwide strikes and a popular uprising
the 1st party congress of the SED
210.context: On 17 June 1953 strikes and a popular uprising spread across the GDR. Soviet tanks put it down.

211.text: Which politician is associated with the "Eastern Treaties"?
211.context: Willy Brandt's government negotiated the Eastern Treaties of the early 1970s, which sought reconciliation with the Soviet Union, Poland and the GDR.

212.context: The country's full name is Bundesrepublik Deutschland, the Federal Republic of Germany.

213.text: How many inhabitants does Germany have?
213.context: Germany has around 84 million inhabitants, making it the most populous country in the European Union.

214.text: What colours does the German flag have?
214.context: The German flag is black, red and gold. The colours go back to the 19th-century movement for a free and united Germany.

215.text: Who is referred to as the "Chancellor of German Unity"?
215.context: Helmut Kohl is called the "Chancellor of German Unity" because reunification was achieved during his time in office in 1990.

216.text: Which symbol can be seen in the plenary chamber of the German Bundestag?
options: the flag of the city of Berlin
216.context: The plenary chamber of the Bundestag is dominated by the Bundesadler, the federal eagle, known informally as the "fat hen".

217.text: During which period did the German Democratic Republic (GDR) exist?
217.context: The GDR existed from 1949 to 1990, just over forty years.

218.text: How many federal states joined the Federal Republic of Germany on reunification in 1990?
218.context: Five federal states joined the Federal Republic in 1990, bringing the total from 11 to 16.

219.text: The Federal Republic of Germany has had its present borders since …
219.context: Germany has had its present borders since reunification in 1990, confirmed by the Two Plus Four Treaty.

220.text: 27 January is an official day of remembrance in Germany. What does this day commemorate?
options: the end of the Second World War
the adoption of the Basic Law
the victims of National Socialism (the day the Auschwitz extermination camp was liberated)
220.context: 27 January is the day Auschwitz was liberated in 1945. It is Germany's official day of remembrance for the victims of National Socialism.

221.text: Germany is a member of the Schengen Agreement. What does that mean?
options: Germans can travel to many countries in Europe without passport checks.
Anyone can enter Germany without identity checks.
Germans can travel to any country without passport checks.
Germans can pay with the euro in any country.
221.context: Schengen means Germans can travel to many European countries without passport checks at the border. It does not abolish identity checks altogether.

222.text: Which country is a neighbour of Germany?
222.context: Switzerland borders Germany in the south. Germany has nine neighbours in all — more than any other EU country.

223.text: Which country is a neighbour of Germany?
223.context: Poland is Germany's eastern neighbour, along the Oder and Neisse rivers.

224.text: What does the abbreviation EU stand for?
224.context: EU stands for European Union, the association of 27 European states.

225.text: In which other country is there a large German-speaking population?
225.context: Austria is German-speaking. German is also an official language in Switzerland, Liechtenstein, Luxembourg and Belgium.

226.text: Which is the flag of the European Union?
226.context: The EU flag is a circle of twelve golden stars on a blue ground. The twelve stands for completeness, not for the number of member states.

227.text: Which country is a neighbour of Germany?
227.context: Denmark is Germany's only northern neighbour, bordering Schleswig-Holstein.

228.text: What is the accession of the GDR to the Federal Republic of Germany in 1990 generally called?
228.context: The accession of the GDR in 1990 is generally called German reunification, die deutsche Wiedervereinigung.

229.text: Which country is a neighbour of Germany?
229.context: Luxembourg borders Germany in the west, next to Rhineland-Palatinate and Saarland.

230.text: The European Parliament is elected regularly, namely every …
230.context: The European Parliament is elected every five years. Every EU citizen may vote, and may do so in their country of residence.

231.text: What does the term "European integration" mean?
options: It refers to American immigrants in Europe.
The term means a halt to immigration into Europe.
It refers to European emigrants in the USA.
The term means the joining together of European states to form the EU.
231.context: European integration means European states joining together ever more closely, a process that led to today's EU.

232.text: Who is elected in the European election?
options: the countries allowed to join the EU
the members of the European Parliament
232.context: The European election chooses the members of the European Parliament. The Commission is not elected by voters directly.

233.text: Which country is a neighbour of Germany?
233.context: Czechia borders Germany in the south-east, along Bavaria and Saxony.

234.text: Where is one seat of the European Parliament?
234.context: Strasbourg is a seat of the European Parliament, which holds its plenary sessions there.

235.text: The then French President François Mitterrand and the then German Federal Chancellor Helmut Kohl commemorate together in Verdun the dead of both world wars. Which aim of the European Union is made clear at this meeting?
options: freedom to travel to all EU countries
peace and security in the countries of the EU
uniform public holidays in the countries of the EU
235.context: Mitterrand and Kohl commemorating the dead of both world wars together at Verdun stands for the EU's central aim: lasting peace and security among its members.

236.text: How many member states does the EU have today?
236.context: The EU has 27 member states, following the United Kingdom's departure in 2020.

237.text: In 2007 the 50th anniversary of the "Treaties of Rome" was celebrated. What were the treaties about?
options: the founding of the European Economic Community (EEC)
fixing the Oder-Neisse line as the eastern border
237.context: The Treaties of Rome of 1957 founded the European Economic Community, the forerunner of today's EU.

238.text: In which places does the European Parliament work?
238.context: The European Parliament works in Strasbourg, Luxembourg and Brussels: plenary sessions in Strasbourg, committees in Brussels, administration in Luxembourg.

239.text: Through which treaties did the Federal Republic of Germany join with other states to form the European Economic Community?
239.context: The Federal Republic joined the European Economic Community through the Treaties of Rome in 1957, as one of the six founding members.

240.text: Since when has cash been paid in euros in Germany?
240.context: Euro notes and coins have been in use in Germany since 1 January 2002. The euro had existed as book money since 1999.

241.text: Ms Seger is having a baby. What does she have to do to receive parental allowance?
options: She has to write to her health insurance fund.
She has to submit an application to the parental allowance office.
She does not have to do anything, because she receives parental allowance automatically.
She has to ask the employment office for permission.
241.context: Parental allowance must be applied for at the Elterngeldstelle. It is not paid automatically.

242.text: Who decides whether a child in Germany goes to kindergarten?
242.context: Parents or legal guardians decide whether their child goes to kindergarten. There is an entitlement to a place from the age of one, but no obligation.

243.text: Maik and Sybille want to hold a demonstration in the street with friends where they live in Germany. What do they have to do beforehand?
options: They have to register the demonstration.
They do not have to do anything. In Germany you may demonstrate anywhere at any time.
They cannot do anything, because demonstrations are generally banned in Germany.
Maik and Sybille have to found a new association, because only associations may demonstrate.
243.context: A demonstration in public must be registered with the authorities beforehand, normally 48 hours in advance. Registration is a notification, not a request for permission.

244.text: Which school-leaving qualification do you normally need to begin a degree at a university in Germany?
244.context: The Abitur is normally required to begin a degree at a university. There are other routes for people with vocational qualifications.

245.text: Who may not live together as a couple in Germany?
options: Hans (20 years old) and Marie (19 years old)
Tom (20 years old) and Klaus (45 years old)
Sofie (35 years old) and Lisa (40 years old)
Anne (13 years old) and Tim (25 years old)
245.context: A 13-year-old may not live with an adult as a partner; children are protected by law. The other pairs are all adults and free to choose.

246.text: At what age do you come of age in Germany?
246.context: You come of age in Germany at 18. From then on you can sign contracts, vote and decide for yourself where to live.

247.text: A woman is pregnant. She is specially protected by law shortly before and after the birth of her child. What is this protection called?
247.context: The protection is called Mutterschutz. It usually runs from six weeks before birth to eight weeks after, with a ban on dismissal.

248.text: In Germany, bringing up children is above all the task …
248.context: Article 6 of the Basic Law makes bringing up children the natural right and primary duty of parents. The state only supervises.

249.text: Who is mainly responsible for bringing up children in Germany?
249.context: Parents are mainly responsible for bringing up their children. The state steps in only if the child's welfare is at risk.

250.text: In Germany you have the best chance of a well-paid job if you …
options: are a member of a party.
250.context: Good qualifications give the best chance of a well-paid job. Religion, sex or party membership must not decide who is hired.

251.text: If you hit a child in Germany, …
options: it is only the family's business.
you cannot be punished for it.
you can be punished for it.
251.context: Children have a legal right to a non-violent upbringing, so hitting a child is punishable in Germany.

options: you may be married to only one partner at a time.
you can have several spouses at the same time.
you may not marry again if you have been married once.
a woman may not marry again if her husband has died.
252.context: Only one marriage at a time is allowed. Remarriage after divorce or the death of a spouse is entirely possible.

253.text: Where do you have to register if you move house in Germany?
253.context: When you move house you must register at the Einwohnermeldeamt, normally within two weeks.

254.text: In Germany, married couples may divorce. Usually they have to observe the "year of separation". What does that mean?
options: The divorce proceedings last a year.
The spouses are married for a year, then divorce is possible.
The right of access to the children applies for a year.
The spouses live their own separate lives for at least a year. After that, divorce is possible.
254.context: The year of separation means the spouses live separate lives for at least a year before the divorce can go through. It is meant to make sure the decision is final.

255.text: For problems bringing up children, parents in Germany can get help from the …
255.context: The Jugendamt, the youth welfare office, advises and supports parents with problems bringing up their children.

256.text: A married couple want to open a restaurant in Germany. What do they absolutely need for this?
options: approval from the residents' registration office
a restaurant licence from the competent authority
256.context: Running a restaurant requires a Gaststättenerlaubnis from the competent authority, especially where alcohol is served.

257.text: An adult woman wants to catch up on her Abitur in Germany. She can do this at …
257.context: An Abendgymnasium, an evening grammar school, lets adults work towards the Abitur alongside a job.

258.text: What is the youth welfare office in Germany allowed to do?
options: It decides which school the child attends.
It can take a child who is being beaten or going hungry out of the family.
It pays the child benefit to the parents.
It checks whether the child attends a kindergarten.
258.context: The youth welfare office may take a child out of the family if the child is being beaten or neglected. It is a last resort and a court is involved.

259.text: The careers information centre (BIZ) at the Federal Employment Agency in Germany helps with …
259.context: The Berufsinformationszentrum helps with career choices and finding an apprenticeship. It is part of the Federal Employment Agency.

260.text: In Germany, a child at school has …
options: a right to unlimited free time.
260.context: School attendance is compulsory, so a child has a duty to attend. Education in state schools is free of charge.

261.text: A man wants to catch up on his Abitur in Germany at the age of 30. Where can he do this? At …
261.context: An evening grammar school is the usual route for adults who want to take the Abitur later in life.

262.text: What does the principle of equal treatment mean in Germany?
options: No one may be disadvantaged because of a disability, for example.
You may disadvantage other people if there are sufficient personal reasons for it.
No one may sue people if they have been disadvantaged.
It is the law for everyone to donate money to disadvantaged groups every year.
262.context: Equal treatment means nobody may be disadvantaged because of things like disability, origin, sex, religion or age. The General Equal Treatment Act sets this out.

263.text: In Germany, young people are criminally responsible from the age of 14. This means: young people who are 14 or older and break criminal laws …
options: share the punishment with their parents.
263.context: From 14 young people are criminally responsible and can be punished, though under juvenile law, which stresses education over retribution.

264.text: At which festival do people in Germany wear colourful costumes and masks?
264.context: At carnival, and especially on Rose Monday, people wear colourful costumes and masks. The celebrations are biggest in the Rhineland.

265.text: Where do you have to go first in Germany if you want to get married?
265.context: To marry you go first to the Standesamt, the registry office. Only a civil marriage is legally valid in Germany.

266.text: When do the statutory quiet hours at night begin in Germany?
options: when the neighbours go to bed
266.context: Statutory quiet hours run from 10 p.m. to 6 a.m. Noise that disturbs the neighbours is not allowed during that time.

267.text: A young woman in Germany, 22 years old, lives with her boyfriend. The woman's parents do not like this, because they do not approve of the boyfriend. What can the parents do?
options: They have to respect the decision of their adult daughter.
They have the right to bring the daughter back to the parental home.
They can go to the police and report the daughter.
They look for another man for the daughter.
267.context: At 22 the daughter is an adult and decides for herself whom she lives with. Her parents have to respect that.

268.text: A young woman wants to take her driving test. She is afraid of the test because her mother tongue is not German. What is correct?
options: She has to live in Germany for at least ten years before she can take the driving test.
If she does not speak German, she may not have a driving licence.
She has to take the driving test in a country where her language is spoken.
She may be able to take the theory test in her mother tongue. There are more than ten languages to choose from.
268.context: The theory test can be taken in a number of languages besides German, so limited German need not be an obstacle.

269.text: In Germany, children from the age of three until they first start school are entitled to …
options: a place in a sports club.
269.context: From the age of three until they start school, children are entitled to a kindergarten place. Since 2013 the entitlement starts at one.

270.text: The Volkshochschule (adult education centre) in Germany is an institution …
270.context: The Volkshochschule is an adult education centre, offering affordable courses in languages, computing and much else to anyone.

271.text: What is a Christmas custom in Germany?
options: dressing up with masks and costumes
271.context: Decorating a fir tree is the classic German Christmas custom. The tradition spread from Germany around the world.

272.text: Which way of life is not permitted in Germany?
options: A man and a woman are divorced and live with new partners.
A single father lives with his two children.
A man is married to two women at the same time.
272.context: Being married to two people at once is not allowed in Germany. Divorce, same-sex partnership and single parenthood are all perfectly lawful.

273.text: For problems bringing up children in Germany, you go …
273.context: With problems bringing up children you go to the Jugendamt, which advises parents free of charge.

274.text: In Germany you have deliberately opened a letter addressed to another person. What have you disregarded?
274.context: Opening someone else's post deliberately breaches the privacy of correspondence, protected by Article 10 of the Basic Law.

275.text: What do you need for a divorce in Germany?
275.context: A divorce goes through the family court, and you need a lawyer to file the petition. Neither the parents nor the children have to consent.

276.text: What should you do if you are treated badly by your contact person at a German public authority?
options: I have to put up with this treatment.
I can complain to the head of the authority.
276.context: If an official treats you badly you can complain to the head of the authority. Public authorities are answerable for how they treat people.

277.text: A woman who has a two-year-old child applies for a job in Germany. What is an example of discrimination? She does not get the job solely because she …
options: has salary expectations that are too high.
has no experience in this occupation.
277.context: Turning a woman down solely because she is a mother is discrimination. Language skills or lack of experience would be job-related reasons.

278.text: A man in a wheelchair has applied for a job as an accountant. What is an example of discrimination? He does not get the job solely because he …
options: has salary expectations that are too high.
278.context: Refusing someone a desk job solely because he uses a wheelchair is discrimination on grounds of disability, which the General Equal Treatment Act forbids.

279.text: Most blocks of rented flats in Germany have house rules. What do such house rules contain? They state …
options: all the tenants in the building.
rules that all residents have to observe.
the address of the nearest public order office.
279.context: House rules set out what all residents of the building have to observe — quiet hours, use of shared rooms, cleaning duties and so on.

280.text: If you want to challenge an incorrect tax assessment in Germany, you have to …
280.context: Against an incorrect tax assessment you lodge an objection, an Einspruch, normally within one month of receiving it.

281.text: Two friends want to go to a public swimming pool in Germany. Both have dark skin and are therefore not let in. Which right is violated in this situation? The right to …
281.context: Refusing entry because of skin colour violates the right to equal treatment. Racial discrimination is forbidden by the Basic Law and by the Equal Treatment Act.

282.text: Which honorary office must German citizens take on if they are asked to do so?
282.context: German citizens can be required to serve as election helpers. It is one of the few honorary offices you cannot simply decline.

283.text: What do you do if you receive an incorrect bill from a German public authority?
options: I leave the bill lying around.
I lodge an objection with the authority.
I send the bill back to the authority.
I take the bill to the tax office.
283.context: If a bill from an authority is wrong you lodge a formal objection, a Widerspruch, with that authority.

284.text: What you need to be able to do for work will change very quickly in future. What can you do?
options: It does not matter what you learn.
Adults have to go on learning even after their training.
